questions.q: What is the main risk of skipping source analysis and going straight to mapping or tooling decisions?
options: There is no real risk, since mapping can be redone cheaply at any time
Salesforce will reject the load automatically if source analysis wasn't documented
Problems with the source data simply get discovered later, during the load, which is a far more expensive time to learn them
It only matters for migrations involving more than one source system
questions.explain: Source analysis doesn't make source data simpler — skipping it just delays discovering real problems (quirks, bad data, volume issues) until the load itself, instead of during cheap, early planning.

questions.q: A customer's phone number differs between an old CRM and a support ticketing tool. What does this lesson say the project needs before migration design proceeds?
options: A deliberately decided system of record for that data, which may differ field-by-field or object-by-object
Nothing — Salesforce will automatically merge conflicting values on load
Both values should always be loaded side by side into two separate fields
The newer of the two systems always wins by default, without discussion
questions.explain: The system of record has to be deliberately decided, often with input from the people who actually use each source, and it isn't necessarily the same system across every field or object.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly named in this lesson as something a useful source analysis document should capture?
options: The exact Apex trigger order on the target Salesforce org
Known quirks in the source data that long-time users already know about
The final field-mapping spreadsheet for the target org
The Bulk API job Id that will eventually be used for the load
questions.explain: A useful source analysis document covers schema, volume, access mechanics, and known quirks — the messiness and inconsistencies long-time users of the source already know about but haven't written down anywhere.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say data volume and access mechanics belong in source analysis rather than being left until later?
options: Because Salesforce requires volume estimates to be submitted before any sandbox can be created
Because volume and access have no real effect on later planning decisions
Because they are only relevant to the final cutover step, not earlier planning
Because they directly shape later tooling and scope/strategy decisions, so discovering them late forces rework
questions.explain: Both the tooling choice (Lesson 5) and the scope/strategy decision (Lesson 4) depend directly on the volume and access facts established during source analysis, which is why this lesson comes before both.

questions.q: Two legacy systems are being consolidated into one Salesforce org. What does this lesson say about how source analysis should be approached?
options: Only the easiest-to-access system needs to be analyzed; the other can be assumed similar
Source analysis is unnecessary for consolidations since both systems are being retired anyway
Each system should be analyzed independently and then reconciled against the other, not just the more convenient one
The two systems should be merged into a single spreadsheet before any analysis begins
questions.explain: A consolidation requires analyzing each source independently and then reconciling them against each other — skipping the less convenient source just defers the discovery of its problems.
